## Bounded read-only decision audit — MP-06 default-privilege choice

**State confirmed from the three plans + inventory:** All 17 public functions are still postgres-owned (evidence file, functions[] array, every `owner: "postgres"`). MP-06.b.1 (three read-RPC revokes), MP-06.g (table/sequence defaults), MP-06.h (search_path) are all **explicit per-object, transactional** interventions — none touched `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` for functions. The MP-06.b default-privilege section is explicit that this remains open, gated on creator/managed-schema rehearsal that has not happened.

**Why the three options aren't interchangeable here:**

- **Global PUBLIC EXECUTE revoke (postgres-as-creator) + public-schema explicit anon/auth revoke:** the 2026-09-11 experiment already proved a global revoke is *not* scoped to `public` — it changes every schema postgres creates functions in, including `auth`, `storage`, `extensions`, `realtime`, GraphQL. Those are Supabase-managed schemas whose install/upgrade flows are not inventoried yet (MP-06.b explicitly lists this as a prerequisite, not done). Per-schema-only revokes don't cancel the global default and don't remove Postgres's built-in implicit PUBLIC EXECUTE grant — both plans repeat this. This option is unsafe to apply before the deployment-creator/managed-schema inventory exists.
- **Dedicated NOLOGIN app-migration creator with its own defaults:** avoids touching postgres's global defaults, but requires establishing who *actually* creates objects during real (hosted) Supabase migrations, new role/membership/CLI rehearsal, and explicitly must not mass-transfer the 17 existing postgres-owned functions (unauthorized here). No hosted Postgres exists to verify this, and the disposable fixture "lacks a real superuser" and may diverge from hosted identity — this cannot be decided from local evidence alone.
- **Per-function transactional revokes + fail-closed catalog guard:** this is the pattern already executed three times successfully (b.1, g, h) with real two-reset replay parity, catalog-delta proofs, and no global-scope side effects. It's the only option provable end-to-end in the disposable fixture today, and the plan already names a "migration review guard that rejects new unreviewed functions/grants" as a required prerequisite before any default migration is ever executable.

**Recommended next bounded step:** extend the existing per-function/catalog-guard approach — build the fail-closed CI guard that fails when a newly introduced public function lacks a matching explicit REVOKE/GRANT row — rather than attempting either default-privilege architecture now. This requires no hosted access, no ownership change, and is directly testable against the nine/twenty-migration fixture pattern already in use.

**Exact prerequisites before A or B can even be chosen:** (1) inventory the real hosted deployment creator and role memberships (cannot be simulated locally); (2) determine who creates `auth`/`storage`/`extensions` objects during supported Supabase upgrade/install; (3) test candidate global defaults against that flow in isolation; (4) enumerate every intentional public/role function grant first.

**Unacceptable shortcuts:** applying the global PUBLIC revoke without managed-schema testing; treating the disposable fixture's superuser behavior as hosted-equivalent; mass-transferring the 17 postgres-owned functions to a new creator without membership/CLI rehearsal; citing the vendor's schema-only revoke example as sufficient; or declaring MP-06/G1 complete from this audit.
